commenti.body: You're missing the entire point of the movie trying to analyze it like this. The whole point of the way the plot is constructed is that each person has a different, often conflicting version of events both due to the imperfection of memory and their incentive to lie about parts of what happened.

I don’t think I’m missing that. But “eyewitness testimony is useless” isn’t a very profound meaning to attribute to a movie. The versions can conflict but also point to an underlying narrative without ruining the movie. I think that it’s actually less interesting to just have four narratives that can’t be made to fit together in any way, anyone can write a story like that.

> anyone can write a story like that.

Then write a movie that's better than Rashomon. Anyone can do it, right?

One of my favorite movies. But I think you're applying too much to it. I think the answer to "what actually happened?" is likely what is told by the woodcutter at the end. Maybe not entirely you could argue, but I don't think it would have been Kurosawa's intent, and definitely not a film from the time period's intent, to try to lend itself to the sort of thing you're doing here. Its not a mystery film, its making a statement about perspective and personal biases. The woodcutters story serving as the "truth" in juxtaposition to the others is what creates that.

You're the only one attributing that meaning, if you need a four word distillation, try subbing out 'useless' for 'fickle' or 'fragile'.

I agree that it could have been tweaked to allow for a canonical truth without ruining the movie, but it would have been a different movie, and I also don't think it would have had anywhere near the lasting impact it had if it made this change. Just my speculation though. 

I don't read any implication that there is no objective reality, just that we are incapable of observing it with only one brain and two eyes.


I'm trying to figure out your intent and help you out but I also agree with the other replies that you're over analysing, it reminds me of the Simpson's episode where Lisa asks 'what's the sound of one hand clapping', and Bart responds cy clapping his fingers against his palm.

I think this is a bit of the "Seinfeld is unfunny" trope. The story might not seem as interesting or profound for you because it's a 74 year old movie. Countless movies and TV shows have remixed, or parodied its plot. If you described something as having a Rashomon style plot there would be people that understand what that means without having seen the movie.

Even the idea that "eyewitness testimony is useless" isn't something that was always taken as a given. Getting people generally on board with that idea wasn't an instant thing. It was a gradual process throughout the 20th century of fiction and academics questioning it, and this movie was part of that.

I think you totally whiffed on what the movie is about. It’s not a mystery to solve or a whodunnit. It’s a meditation on truth, and how truth can be different from different points of view. 

I’m not saying this applies to you, but there’s that whole YouTube “mystery solved” trend of videos, which totally misses the point of art; art isn’t necessarily something to be solved through hunting for clues. It’s about truth and meaning and what you the viewer can learn about yourself and those around you.

The movie takes the idea that women are manipulative and crazy REALLY far if you read it through this lens. Maybe I’m looking at it through my own modern lens, but I found the woodcutter’s account not as credible - especially as he was established to have been lying for sure. Everyone who is saying I missed the point of the film is somewhat talking down to me, I feel. (Your comment actually feels like I can respond to it without being lectured). But to me the movie showed that people interpret things in self interested ways AND that the legal process involves bias when it comes to testimony. I think it’s VERY plausible that most women would not capitulate to rape or lustily beg a rapist to kill her husband. But the movie assumes that of course this is very likely - the monk is shook like “of course that’s just how people are.” The group of the three guys in the frame story is like “gosh! Women!” Some of the other respondents to my question are scolding me like “why aren’t you a good viewer! You’re supposed to find the woman’s testimony as unreliable as the perpetrator’s!” Through my own lens, it occurred to me that there is no need to do this - in fact it makes the movie distasteful to me, if we are somehow “supposed” to take away some kind of canned message about art.

I mean yes, I understand the point of this famous movie - everyone knows what the thesis of this movie is. But I don’t think the fact that it makes comments about the justice system and the role of bias in testimony is irrelevant. Maybe Kurosawa didn’t intend the woman to be a reliable narrator - maybe we were supposed to think of her as murderous, manipulative and depraved just like all the three men depicted her. But I’m not super pious about feeling how the director wants me to feel. And I can’t tell, because it seems very possible to me that the unrecognized validity of the woman’s plight actually is an intended message in the movie. None of the men in the frame story convey any empathy for her or understanding of the circumstances that would lead her to make the choices they describe her as making. But it’s the central moral drama of the movie - if her word carries weight.

You’re quipping about something I didn’t even say. That’s too mean for my taste. I will let you have this argument- not because you’re right- but I feel like you need it more. I feel like you need there to be an objective meaning to Rashomon that if other people don’t get they’re stupider than you. Like it’s just a feeling. But realistically it’s a movie about subjectivity, so I hope part of you understands that this isn’t a good way to talk to people. I hope some part of you understands that it comes from a place of insecurity.

>The movie takes the idea that women are manipulative and crazy REALLY far if you read it through this lens

Ya, honestly, I do get that. At best, it depicts a woman who is torn between being faithful and manipulating the thief into getting her out of a situation she its implied she doesn't want to be in. At worst, its showing her as genuinely drawn to the man who's about to kidnap her. 

On the former, you can view it through a 'modern lens', but this is a sort of story archetype that is used CONSTANTLY in films all the time, even to this day. Femme fatal - there's a whole genre basically of it. Its a little disingenuous to take an issue with this, because that is to argue that a depiction of a woman being manipulative to the detriment of others is so unrealistic, that its offensive. Women (and men) are manipulative and self serving all the time.
